etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English contenden, borrowed from Old French contendre, from Latin contendere (“to stretch out, extend, strive after, contend”), from com- (“together”) + tendere (“to stretch”); see tend, and compare attend, extend, intend, subtend.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be in opposition; to contest; to dispute; to vie; to quarrel; to fight.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Deuteronomy 2:9:
quote.text: The Lord said unto me, Distress not the Moabites, neither contend with them in battle.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: For never two such kingdoms did contend without much fall of blood.

quote.citation: 2011, Osaiah "Ike" Wilson III, James J.F. Forrest, Handbook of Defence Politics
quote.text: the armies of Syria and Lebanon lack the capability to contend with the Israeli army, as demonstrated during the course of the First Lebanon War.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To struggle or exert oneself to obtain or retain possession of, or to defend.

quote.citation: 17th century, John Dryden, Epistle III to the Lady Castlemain
quote.text: You sit above, and see vain men below / Contend for what you only can bestow.

quote.citation: 2020, C. Matthew McMahon, Therese B. McMahon, 5 Marks of Christian Resolve:
quote.text: God has entrusted something to the church, and it is the church's job to contend for it, even unto death

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be in debate; to engage in discussion; to dispute; to argue.

quote.citation: 1689 (indicated as 1690), [John Locke], chapter 2, in An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding. […], London:  […]  Eliz[abeth] Holt, for Thomas Basset, […], →OCLC, book I, page 9:
quote.text: these simple ideas are far from those innate principles which some contend for

quote.citation: 1667, attributed to Richard Allestree, The Causes of the Decay of Christian Piety. […], London:  […]  R. Norton for T. Garthwait, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: many of those things he so fiercely contended about , were either falle or trivial

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To believe (something is reasonable) and argue (for it); to advocate.

quote.citation: 1996, Michael Adler, Erio Ziglio, Gazing Into the Oracle […] :
quote.text: Some panellists contended that the costs of research and care justified the establishment of a permanent national commission

quote.citation: 2022 August 24, Tassanee Vejpongsa, Grant Peck, “Thai court suspends PM Prayuth pending ruling on term limit”, in The Washington Post‎[1], retrieved 2022-08-24:
quote.text: His critics contend the eight years [term limit] expired Tuesday, the day before the anniversary of Prayuth officially becoming prime minister in the military government installed after the coup.

definitions.definition: contend with: To try to cope with a difficulty or problem.

quote.citation: 2021 December 29, Dominique Louis, “Causal analysis: crashworthiness at Sandilands”, in RAIL, number 947, page 32:
quote.text: However, the challenges for the railway world are much greater than for automotive as we generally have more occupants, higher speeds, greater masses, higher energies, and an absence of seatbelts or airbags to contend with.
